21       Before the Court is a Motion to Compel filed by Plaintiff Christopher Vopatek 
22  (“Plaintiff”).    (ECF No.  50.)    Plaintiff  moves to  compel Defendant USAA  Casualty 
23  Insurance Company (“Defendant” or “USAA”) to respond to Request for Production 
24  (“RFP”) Nos. 21 and 22 and Plaintiff’s Interrogatory Nos. 11 and 12.  (Id. at 2.)  Defendant 
25  filed an opposition (ECF No. 53), and Plaintiff filed a reply with an expert declaration 
26  (ECF No. 55).  Defendant objected to Plaintiff’s expert’s declaration (ECF No. 56) and 
27  filed a supplemental declaration in response (ECF No. 63).  Plaintiff thereafter objected to 
28  Defendant’s supplemental declaration.  (ECF No. 64.)                      
1       On July 18, 2025, the Court held a hearing on the Motion to Compel.  (ECF No. 65.)  
2  Following the hearing, the Court ordered Defendant to supplement its opposition and gave 
3  Plaintiff an opportunity to respond to the legal authority presented by Defendant at the 
4  hearing.  (ECF No. 67.)  Plaintiff thereafter filed a reply addressing Defendant’s cited legal 
5  authority (ECF No. 72), and Defendant filed three supplemental declarations (ECF Nos. 
6  78–80, 83).  For the reasons set forth below, the Court GRANTS IN PART and DENIES 
7  IN PART Plaintiff’s Motion to Compel.                                     
8  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
9       Plaintiff commenced this action against USAA on June 30, 2023.  (ECF No. 1 
10  (“Compl.”).)  Plaintiff had an automobile insurance policy with USAA, Policy No. 00951 
11  78 46C 7103 3, effective September 19, 2017, through September 19, 2020 (the “Policy”).  
12  (Compl. ¶ 7.)  On April 4, 2020, Plaintiff was driving his insured vehicle while working 
13  for Uber Eats deliveries.  (Id. ¶ 13.)  After logging out of his Uber application for the night, 
14  Plaintiff was involved in a head-on motor vehicle accident with an intoxicated driver 
15  wherein he suffered severe personal injuries and property damage.  (Id. ¶¶ 14–17.)  The 
16  other driver was at fault.  (Id. ¶¶ 18–19.)  The at-fault driver’s policy limit was $15,000 per 
17  person and $30,000 per accident.  (Id. ¶ 36.)  The at-fault driver’s insurer tendered its policy 
18  limits of $15,000 to Plaintiff.  (Id. ¶ 21.)                              
19       Plaintiff  thereafter  submitted  a  claim  to  USAA  seeking  uninsured 
20  motorist/underinsured motorist (“UM/UIM”) coverage on the ground he suffered bodily 
21  injury and property damage due to the sole fault of an underinsured motorist.  (Id. ¶ 24.)  
22  The UM/UIM limits of Plaintiff’s Policy were $300,000.00 per person and $500,000.00 
23  per accident.  (Id. ¶¶ 7, 23.)  USAA denied coverage on the ground that the Policy does not 
24  pay for a loss to a covered auto “which occurs while it is being used to carry persons for a 
25  fee.”  (Id. ¶¶ 25–26.)  Plaintiff thereafter renewed his demand, which was denied again 
26  because USAA claimed, without producing evidence, that Plaintiff “was confirmed to be 
27  in active status on his ride share application at the time of the accident.”  (Id. ¶¶ 27–29.)  
28  Plaintiff was not logged in to the Uber Eats application at the time of the accident.  (Id. ¶¶ 
1  29–32.)  Plaintiff brings causes of action for breach of contract, breach of implied covenant 
2  of good faith and fair dealing, and declaratory relief.  (Id. at 9–14.)   
3       On February 26, 2024, the Honorable Roger T. Benitez granted the parties’ joint 
4  motion to stay the action pending the outcome of mandatory UIM arbitration.  (ECF No. 
5  25.)  During the stay, a settlement was reached as to the parties’ dispute regarding the 
6  amount of UIM benefits owed to Plaintiff.  (ECF No. 31 at 2.)  On October 1, 2024, the 
7  parties informed the Court that their settlement of the underlying UIM claim had been 
8  finalized.    (ECF  No.  33  at  2.)    The  Honorable  Cynthia  Bashant  lifted  the  stay  on 
9  October 7, 2024, and issued a new schedule.  (ECF No. 35.)                
10  II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                      
11       Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b), a party is entitled to seek discovery of 
12  “any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional 
13  to the needs of the case, considering the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the 
14  amount in controversy, the parties’ relative access to relevant information, the parties’ 
15  resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues, and whether the burden 
16  or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
17  26(b)(1).  Information need not be admissible to be discoverable.  Id.    
18       “The party seeking to compel discovery has the burden of establishing that its request 
19  satisfies the relevancy requirements of Rule 26(b)(1).”  Alves v. Riverside Cnty., 339 F.R.D. 
20  556, 559 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (quoting Bryant v. Ochoa, No. 07-CV-00200-JM-PCL, 2009 
21  WL 1390794, at *1 (S.D. Cal. May 14, 2009)).  “District courts have broad discretion in 
22  determining relevancy for discovery purposes.”  Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 
23  406 F.3d 625, 635 (9th Cir. 2005) (citing Hallett v. Morgan, 296 F.3d 732, 751 (9th Cir. 
24  2002)).    “Once  the  propounding  party  establishes  that  the  request  seeks  relevant 
25  information, ‘[t]he party who resists discovery has the burden to show discovery should 
26  not  be  allowed,  and  has  the  burden  of  clarifying,  explaining,  and  supporting  its 
27  objections.’”  Goro v. Flowers Foods, Inc., 334 F.R.D. 275, 283 (S.D. Cal. 2018) (quoting 
28  Superior Commc’ns v. Earhugger, Inc., 257 F.R.D. 215, 217 (C.D. Cal. 2009)).  However, 
1  a court must—either on motion or sua sponte—“limit the frequency or extent” of otherwise 
2  permissible discovery if the court finds, inter alia, the request “unreasonably cumulative 
3  or  duplicative”  or  the  discovery  sought  is  obtainable  from  a  “more  convenient,  less 
4  burdensome, or less expensive” source.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(C)(i).   
5  III.   DISCUSSION                                                         
6       A.    Relevant Background                                            
7       In his motion, Plaintiff claims that, in the days after the April 4, 2020 accident, 
8  USAA never asked him any questions about his ride sharing activity.  (ECF No. 50 at 4.)  
9  After the initial denial on May 19, 2020, Plaintiff’s counsel immediately disputed the 
10  denial, reiterating that Plaintiff was not logged in to the Uber Eats application at the time 
11  of the accident and that Plaintiff’s counsel was told USAA had not spoken with Uber about 
12  the issue.  (Id.)  Counsel asked for all evidence on which USAA was basing its denial.  (Id.)  
13  USAA provided an April 9, 2020 email from Uber to an adjuster for Progressive Insurance 
14  (“Progressive”), Uber’s group insurance carrier for its drivers, which asserted, “Our data 
15  confirms the driver was in P1/Available on the reported loss street, Gopher Canyon Rd 
16  near the reported time of loss.”  (Id. at 5; ECF No. 50-1 at 35; see also ECF No. 53 at 11.)  
17  Plaintiff claims that there was “no discussion regarding the precise times, locations, and 
18  app status of Plaintiff in relation to the time of loss by anyone,” and that USAA did not 
19  receive this April 9 email until a day after it issued its denial on May 19.  (Id. at 5.)  Plaintiff 
20  further claims that USAA never contacted Uber directly.  (Id.)  Plaintiff asserts that it was 
21  only after he was forced to file this bad faith action that USAA finally sought the driver 
22  activity log from Uber.  (Id.)  The log ultimately obtained from Uber showed that Plaintiff 
23  was not logged in at the time of the accident and coverage was in fact owed.  (Id.) 
24       USAA disputes Plaintiff’s version of events.  USAA claims that two days after the 
25  April 4 accident, Plaintiff provided a recorded statement to USAA, but this statement was 
26  not used in determining whether to deny coverage.  (ECF Nos. 53 at 3–4; 53-1 at 67.)  On 
27  April 8, an adjuster from Progressive contacted USAA and advised the company that a 
28  separate claim had been opened with Progressive on Plaintiff’s behalf because he was 
1  driving for Uber Eats at the time of the accident.  (ECF No. 53 at 4; see also ECF No. 50-
2  1 at 21.)  On April 10, USAA called Plaintiff to ask if he was driving for Uber Eats at the 
3  time of the accident.  (Id.)  Plaintiff stated that he had finished working for Uber Eats and 
4  was on his way to a friend’s house when the accident happened.  (Id.; see also ECF No. 
5  53-1 at 60.)  Plaintiff thought he was “clocked out” out of Uber Eats, but while he was 
6  sitting at the side of the road after the accident, he received multiple delivery assignments, 
7  and even at the hospital, he continued to receive calls regarding deliveries.  (Id.; see also 
8  ECF No. 53-1 at 60.)                                                      
9       Progressive advised USAA on May 8 that Plaintiff was classified by Uber as being 
10  in Phase 1 (or Period 1) at the time of the accident, meaning his Uber Eats application was 
11  turned on and waiting for a rider or delivery notification.  (Id.; see also ECF No. 53-1 at 
12  63.)    Pursuant  to  the  rideshare  provisions  of  the  Policy,  and  based  upon  Plaintiff’s, 
13  Progressive’s,  and  Uber’s  statements  to  USAA,  USAA  claims  that  it  “believed  that 
14  Plaintiff’s claim was not covered,” and denied coverage.  (Id.; see also ECF No. 53-1 at 
15  67.)  After receiving more information, including the “activity log with GPS coordinates 
16  and sign on/sign off times” on October 20, 2023, via subpoena, USAA determined that 
17  Plaintiff “was not in an active or available status on the application at the time of the 
18  accident.”  (ECF No. 53-1 at 69–76.)  On January 9, 2024, USAA accepted Plaintiff’s 
19  claim.  (Id. at 75–76.)

20       C.    Analysis                                                       
21       By means of the foregoing discovery requests, Plaintiff seeks pattern and practice 
22  discovery  relating  to  USAA  insureds  seeking  UM/UIM  coverage  where  ride  sharing 
23  activity was disputed, as well as complaints from insureds that USAA did not properly 
24  investigate ride sharing activity.  (ECF No. 50 at 2.)  Plaintiff believes that the evidence 
25  will show that USAA “regularly failed to obtain the driver log when investigating disputed 
26  ride sharing activity[,]” although required to do so by USAA’s internal guidelines and 
27  industry standards.  (Id. at 2–4.)  With this information, Plaintiff argues that he can establish 
28  bad faith and support punitive damages by way of pattern and practice.  (Id. at 2.)  Plaintiff 
1  points to his own inability to obtain the log from Uber, along with USAA’s statement that 
2  “Uber reps do not take direct contact . . . [t]hey are very difficult to reach,” and the fact 
3  USAA never contacted Uber once while investigating Plaintiff’s claim, as indicators that 
4  it is “highly likely, if not certain, that USAA routinely does not obtain the driver log where 
5  ride sharing activity is disputed and wrongfully shifts the burden and duty to investigate to 
6  its insureds.”  (Id. at 2–3.)                                             
7       In his Complaint, Plaintiff brings a cause of action for breach of the implied covenant 
8  of good faith and fair dealing and seeks punitive damages.  (Compl. ¶¶ 54–66.)  To support 
9  his breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing cause of action, Plaintiff 
10  alleges that USAA breached its obligation to act fairly and in good faith by, inter alia, 
11  “[u]nreasonably asserting Plaintiff was logged in to the UBER application at the time of 
12  the  accident  while  lacking  any  evidence  of  such  fact,”  “[u]nreasonably  relying  on 
13  unverified  and  unconfirmed  statements  from  third  parties  to  exclude  coverage,”  and 
14  “[u]nreasonably, intentionally and willfully, with full knowledge and the intent to deceive 
15  and deprive Plaintiff of benefits owed pursuant to the Policy, fraudulently fabricating and 
16  manufacturing facts without any supporting evidence in order to deny coverage.”  (Id. ¶ 
17  60(a)–(c).)  Plaintiff further alleges that USAA breached its obligation to act fairly and in 
18  good faith by “[e]mbarking on a course of conduct and pattern and practice wherein 
19  Defendant would fail to provide any legal support for its positions regarding application of 
20  exclusions to the claim and/or fail to acknowledge coverage owed,” and by “[p]ursuing 
21  such a course of conduct and pattern and practice in violation of the terms of the Policy 
22  and  California  law  with  the  knowledge,  understanding,  consent  and  approval  of 
23  Defendant’s managing officers, directors, agents and employees.”  (Id.)   
24       California law “implies in every contract, including insurance policies, a covenant 
25  of good faith and fair dealing.”  Wilson v. 21st Century Ins. Co., 42 Cal. 4th 713, 720 
26  (2007), as modified (Dec. 19, 2007).  “Therefore, when an insurer unreasonably and in bad 
27  faith withholds payment on a claim of its insured, it is subject to liability in tort.”  Downey 
28  Sav. & Loan Assn. v. Ohio Cas. Ins. Co., 189 Cal. App. 3d 1072, 1096 (1987).  “An insurer 
1  may also breach the covenant of good faith and fair dealing when it fails to properly 
2  investigate its insured’s claim.”  McCoy v. Progressive W. Ins. Co., 171 Cal. App. 4th 785, 
3  792–93 (2009) (citation omitted).  Under this implied promise, in determining whether to 
4  settle a claim, the insurer must give “at least as much consideration to the welfare of its 
5  insured as it gives to its own interests.”  Egan v. Mut. of Omaha Ins. Co., 24 Cal. 3d 809, 
6  818 (1979).                                                               
7       Plaintiff relies on Colonial Life & Accident Ins. Co. v. Superior Court, 31 Cal. 3d 
8  785 (1982), to support his contention that discovery regarding other claims handled by 
9  USAA is relevant to his bad faith and punitive damages claims.  (ECF No. 50 at 2, 5–6, 7–
10  9.)  Indeed, a bad faith claim may be established “by showing either that the acts that 
11  harmed [the plaintiff] were knowingly committed or were engaged in with such frequency 
12  as to indicate a general business practice.”  Colonial Life, 31 Cal. 3d at 791; accord Shenon 
13  v. New York Life Ins. Co., No. 2:18 CV 00240, 2021 WL 4804053, at *3 n.2 (C.D. Cal. 
14  Oct. 14, 2021).  Moreover, “[o]ther instances of alleged unfair settlement practices may 
15  also be highly relevant to [a] plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages.”  Colonial Life, 31 
16  Cal. 3d at 791.  Thus, “the elements of punitive damages may be suggested by a pattern of 
17  unfair  practices.”    Id.  at  792.    Accordingly,  “[d]iscovery  aimed  at  determining  the 
18  frequency of alleged unfair settlement practices is . . . likely to produce evidence directly 
19  relevant to [a bad faith] action.”  Id. at 791.                           
20       “Although Colonial Life is not binding in discovery disputes in federal court, it 
21  provides helpful guidance about relevance in connection with allegations of an insurer’s 
22  breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing under California law.”  Kahlenberg 
23  v. Bamboo IDE8 Ins. Servs., LLC, No. 2:20-cv-06805-FLA-PDx, 2021 WL 8693114, at *3 
24  (C.D. Cal. May 19, 2021).  Indeed, “Colonial Life . . . has been cited by California state 
25  and federal courts for the idea that an insurer’s handling of other claims is relevant to 
26  punitive damages and common law ‘bad faith’ claims.”  Van Duyn v. Am. Sec. Ins. Co.,

20       C.    Analysis                                                       
21       By means of the foregoing discovery requests, Plaintiff seeks pattern and practice 
22  discovery  relating  to  USAA  insureds  seeking  UM/UIM  coverage  where  ride  sharing 
23  activity was disputed, as well as complaints from insureds that USAA did not properly 
24  investigate ride sharing activity.  (ECF No. 50 at 2.)  Plaintiff believes that the evidence 
25  will show that USAA “regularly failed to obtain the driver log when investigating disputed 
26  ride sharing activity[,]” although required to do so by USAA’s internal guidelines and 
27  industry standards.  (Id. at 2–4.)  With this information, Plaintiff argues that he can establish 
28  bad faith and support punitive damages by way of pattern and practice.  (Id. at 2.)  Plaintiff 
1  points to his own inability to obtain the log from Uber, along with USAA’s statement that 
2  “Uber reps do not take direct contact . . . [t]hey are very difficult to reach,” and the fact 
3  USAA never contacted Uber once while investigating Plaintiff’s claim, as indicators that 
4  it is “highly likely, if not certain, that USAA routinely does not obtain the driver log where

6  its insureds.”  (Id. at 2–3.)                                             
7       In his Complaint, Plaintiff brings a cause of action for breach of the implied covenant 
8  of good faith and fair dealing and seeks punitive damages.  (Compl. ¶¶ 54–66.)  To support 
9  his breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing cause of action, Plaintiff 
10  alleges that USAA breached its obligation to act fairly and in good faith by, inter alia, 
11  “[u]nreasonably asserting Plaintiff was logged in to the UBER application at the time of 
12  the  accident  while  lacking  any  evidence  of  such  fact,”  “[u]nreasonably  relying  on 
13  unverified  and  unconfirmed  statements  from  third  parties  to  exclude  coverage,”  and 
14  “[u]nreasonably, intentionally and willfully, with full knowledge and the intent to deceive 
15  and deprive Plaintiff of benefits owed pursuant to the Policy, fraudulently fabricating and 
16  manufacturing facts without any supporting evidence in order to deny coverage.”  (Id. ¶ 
17  60(a)–(c).)  Plaintiff further alleges that USAA breached its obligation to act fairly and in 
18  good faith by “[e]mbarking on a course of conduct and pattern and practice wherein 
19  Defendant would fail to provide any legal support for its positions regarding application of 
20  exclusions to the claim and/or fail to acknowledge coverage owed,” and by “[p]ursuing 
21  such a course of conduct and pattern and practice in violation of the terms of the Policy 
22  and  California  law  with  the  knowledge,  understanding,  consent  and  approval  of 
23  Defendant’s managing officers, directors, agents and employees.”  (Id.)   
24       California law “implies in every contract, including insurance policies, a covenant 
25  of good faith and fair dealing.”  Wilson v. 21st Century Ins. Co.,
42 Cal. 4th 713
, 720 
26  (2007), as modified (Dec. 19, 2007).  “Therefore, when an insurer unreasonably and in bad 
27  faith withholds payment on a claim of its insured, it is subject to liability in tort.”  Downey 
28  Sav. & Loan Assn. v. Ohio Cas. Ins. Co.,
189 Cal. App. 3d 1072, 1096
 (1987).  “An insurer 
1  may also breach the covenant of good faith and fair dealing when it fails to properly 
2  investigate its insured’s claim.”  McCoy v. Progressive W. Ins. Co.,
171 Cal. App. 4th 785
, 
3  792–93 (2009) (citation omitted).  Under this implied promise, in determining whether to 
4  settle a claim, the insurer must give “at least as much consideration to the welfare of its 
5  insured as it gives to its own interests.”  Egan v. Mut. of Omaha Ins. Co.,
24 Cal. 3d 809
, 
6  818 (1979).                                                               
7       Plaintiff relies on Colonial Life & Accident Ins. Co. v. Superior Court,
31 Cal. 3d 8
  785 (1982), to support his contention that discovery regarding other claims handled by 
9  USAA is relevant to his bad faith and punitive damages claims.  (ECF No. 50 at 2, 5–6, 7–
10  9.)  Indeed, a bad faith claim may be established “by showing either that the acts that 
11  harmed [the plaintiff] were knowingly committed or were engaged in with such frequency 
12  as to indicate a general business practice.”  Colonial Life, 31 Cal. 3d at 791; accord Shenon 
13  v. New York Life Ins. Co., No. 2:18 CV 00240,
2021 WL 4804053
, at *3 n.2 (C.D. Cal. 
14  Oct. 14, 2021).  Moreover, “[o]ther instances of alleged unfair settlement practices may 
15  also be highly relevant to [a] plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages.”  Colonial Life, 31 
16  Cal. 3d at 791.  Thus, “the elements of punitive damages may be suggested by a pattern of 
17  unfair  practices.”    Id.  at  792.    Accordingly,  “[d]iscovery  aimed  at  determining  the 
18  frequency of alleged unfair settlement practices is . . . likely to produce evidence directly 
19  relevant to [a bad faith] action.”  Id. at 791.                           
20       “Although Colonial Life is not binding in discovery disputes in federal court, it 
21  provides helpful guidance about relevance in connection with allegations of an insurer’s 
22  breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing under California law.”  Kahlenberg 
23  v. Bamboo IDE8 Ins. Servs., LLC, No. 2:20-cv-06805-FLA-PDx,
2021 WL 8693114
, at *3 
24  (C.D. Cal. May 19, 2021).  Indeed, “Colonial Life . . . has been cited by California state 
25  and federal courts for the idea that an insurer’s handling of other claims is relevant to 
26  punitive damages and common law ‘bad faith’ claims.”  Van Duyn v. Am. Sec. Ins. Co., 
27  No. CV 08-5748-GW(CTX),
2009 WL 10672575
, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Apr. 14, 2009); see, 
28  e.g., Moore v. American United Life Ins. Co.,
150 Cal. App. 3d 610
 (1984) (noting 
1  information regarding non-party insureds’ settlement attempts is relevant to common law 
2  bad faith claim); J & M Assocs., Inc. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, PA, No. 
3  06-CV-0903-W (JMA),
2008 WL 638137
, at *4–5 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 4, 2008) (finding that 
4  Colonial Life applies whether bad faith is alleged under a statute or under a common law 
5  theory).
